content:
I wish to address an issue of relevance to all CSLib contributors. There currently appears to be significant ambiguity in how attribution and authorship works in this community. This affects us all if not addressed soon.  

To take one example, it is extremely unclear what happens if someone decides to open a PR that practically replicates the ideas and much of the implementation of an older ongoing PR. This PR takes all the ideas, and presents a superficially modified implementation while the author of the new PR claims (first) authorship and copyright. Any one of us could work for months or years to fructify their ideas only to find that a different contributor has adopted it all and made a fresh pr, claiming copyright, (even@ first) authorship and credit for themselves. It seems at present that even in such a situation, the new PR can be merged instead of the original.  

I believe none of us would like to contribute to a project if credit for our work could be taken away from us or diminished so easily. It is fundamentally a question of ethics and respecting authorship of both ideas and implementation. This is especially true in CSLib where so many of us come from academic backgrounds and are trying to find the best formalisations for our field and contribute them to cslib to build a coherent library. In many cases we are inventing formalisations from scratch for entire sub fields of CS that haven’t seen formalisation before. This is publishable and original work. Therefore authorship and copyright are very important for us. I will highlight a specific instance in a separate spoiler message.

My personal example

If you consider this  farfetched, I'd like to bring your attention to an example where it happened to me recently. For years, preceding even the debate formalisation framework by months, I have been developing and discussing a formalisation idea for algorithms theory that is reliant on a more abstract parametric model than the conventional models of computation so many of us learn in undergrad. It has been important to build social consensus on this idea as much as technical. It separates the basic operations we care to count and the combinators that we use on top of them which gives a structural way of computing the real complexity costs of an algorithm. Briefly it is meant to allow a top-down formalisation of algorithms that makes it viable to modularly separate an algorithm from its dependencies in the literature. It also lets us talk about computational models independently of algorithms written with them.I have called it by several names on Zulip, discord, and my chats with algorithms researchers, including the query model, query combinator model, and most recently Prog. Thanks to Tanner Duve, I recently learnt that I could outsource the combinator part of this idea to monads using their implementation of Free monads. Since then, after lengthy prior Zulip discussions in this channel, I have been building this framework for you months, first in cslib#275, subsequently in cslib#372, and then some further extensions. I have discovered that I can encode models well beyond traditional sequential algorithms in my framework. cslib#372 received approval for merging on the morning of 27th February, just hours before I presented it at a talk.  

However since then a senior member of this community has seen fit to make, at first a competing PR that they claimed implemented the query complexity model (note my idea). The PR was made with no prior discussion unlike mine. They claimed  (initially without substantiation) that it was better than mine. I spent days systematically refuting their more reasoned claims. At one point they claimed that I couldn’t state a lower bound theorem. In response, and amid a research workshop, I supplied a somewhat rough GPT-assisted proof of this theorem in my PR. Hours later they produced a lower bound proof that used my model instead of theirs in their PR. Subsequently upon suggestion by another contributor here, we agreed to a joint effort that was supposed to combine the benefits of our models. A key observation was that my model was indeed usable for both upper and lower bounds in algorithms, a significant retraction of their previous claims. Instead of collaborating, they made a fresh pr. This PR remains incomplete, and already substantially borrows both my ideas and code. Should it address all the technical concerns about it, it will be a superficial replacement of my pr. Concretely, it does not meaningfully improve my PR as of now.

Yet I (and my coauthors) have been denied (first) authorship and copyright on all files of this PR and added as a last author in a handful of files. I am also denied authorship of my own idea of using query models as a universal algorithmic meta-model, to which, based on the last two weeks, I can safely say that the author of this PR has made no relevant contribution. They may have made an entirely separate PR and there may be superficial differences in code (in particular, certain redundant types in the lower bound proof, definitions, and styles of statements).  

I am a phd student trying to fructify a research programme for algorithms formalisation into a concrete framework. When someone takes my work and denies my authorship it hurts my career. Further I am actively working with algorithms theorists on research problems in this area, and came up with this solution after years of engaging with the literature of the community. I can’t imagine any of us would be happy to be in such a situation.

Therefore I ask the community to clarify how authorship and credit works. It would be of help to all of us in this community and give clarity on how we should proceed with contributions. This is especially the case when a new implementation is being experimented on and built as will be the case in many areas of CS which have never seen formalisation before, which might lead to publishable work.

Here's what the mathlib style guide has to say about Authors:

Regarding the list of authors: [...] We don't have strict rules on what contributions qualify for inclusion there. The general idea is that the people listed there should be the ones we would reach out to if we had questions about the design or development of the Lean code.
I am speaking about authorship in both an academic sense and the mathlib style guide sense, both of which i think are relevant in the case of CSLib as I have argued above.

I want to clarify that

cslib#372 received approval for merging on the morning of 27th February

was me who approved. I did so in response to a few small technical points that were addressed, not the overall work, as I specified on the review. While I have some extra approval permissions because of helping with releases, I am not an expert in this area and defer to the lead maintainer (Fabrizio) for new efforts where we don't yet have an established maintainer.

I'd like to note that the more recent PRs you mention were both opened as drafts, and a thread was opened (#CSLib > Algorithm frameworks (TimeM, cslib#372, cslib#376) ) to discuss comparing them technically. Most importantly none of these have been merged and nobody else as far as I am aware has mentioned any intent of pursuing academic authorship. I am also a PhD student, and I understand the stress and importance of authorship. To me this has all looked like well-intentioned experimentation and discussion while trying to nail down design decisions.

I believe the authorship norms situation is still unclear. It is unclear about overlapping PRs being opened where the whole idea is taken from the earlier PR while the OG author is reduced to final authorship in a fraction of the files and the new author has inserted themselves. Some clear norms, that require prior discussion of an overlapping PR or even requiring that new PRs be made on top of existing PRs with such overlap (as should be the case), would give us a lot of clarity.

About personal example

This looks more like experimentation on my idea with what it largely looks like my code + extensions and seems (per pr comments) poised to converge more.

  1. About my extension PRs. Hence I refer to them as extensions.

  2. Even in experimentation I did not delete or change author names on other files. I even put a comment in the mergeSort file noting where I used sorrachai’s code to show similarity of my mergeSort examplewith his for comparison.

  3. I also did not open the PR before sufficient discussions in advance. This is something that’s considered basic etiquette in OSS. I enforced this in the equational theories project. A mathlib moderator helped me out by enforcing this etiquette in the port to avoid overwriting and duplicating PRs. Clearly this is a norm in this community.

  4. When Eric and you pointed out that I could re use TimeM code instead of writing my owing timing procedures from scratch , I hesitated a lot as you recall, but eventually I admitted and accepted it. I also did not outright delete TimeM or make a PR before TimeM was merged.

At no point did I spring the PR as a surprise to another contributor and make it a copy of another PR while throwing silly challenges to the other. I also didn’t take the basic idea from another contributor.

I can say none of the above for the other PR.

I even suggested to this alt PR author to make a pr against mine and improve it. This is basic collaboration etiquette in academia. If B learns of an idea from someone else (let’s say A) and wish to improve it, B can’t submit their own draft preprint without A. B collaborates with A or if A turns them down then B publishes their own part as follow up work . Likewise in OSS, one first discusses improvements, not make competing PRs. I accepted joint work in good faith, and now find myself in this situation. Fair experimentation and collaboration in this instance would have meant working on top of my PR. Not building a parallel one.

a bit more on the specific instance

A final point to note. Even if nobody discussed any intent to publish their version of the idea, it becomes a problem for me, because the mainstream version of the idea has their name all over it. Both from an authorship norms and copyright perspective.

I am aware that these are still draft PRs. I am raising this issue right now because, draft or not, they are still different PRs and in their current state only one of them can be merged. Which means the lack of clarity on authorship norms directly impacts us. In this case, at present, it also affects who gets (first) authorship and copyright.

about discussing design decisions

I also wish to point out that no current issue has been identified with cslib#372 that is addressed by cslib#401. With its existing code and comments provided by reviewers other than me, it will resemble mine even more.

That being said, experimentation with design requires a proper prior discussion. From the beginning I have been subject to false claim after false claim and challenges, all of which I have addressed. Since 401, I have made a number of comments about its design. None of which have been addressed. This experimentation has not produced substantially different designs as of this point.

This is all not including the complete ignoring of basic norms in OSS where contributors first discuss their proposal, and avoid creating duplicating PRs. A nice and important side-effect of these norms is that the authorship order and copyright is preserved in the main branch.

I agree that we would benefit from a more explicit policy on authorship especially as the community is growing quickly and AI lowers the boundary of creating new PRs. Many of us are young researchers who do not want to waste months working on a feature that doesn't make it due to someone else opening a similar PR, our careers are already in a sensitive spot and such incidents can cause harm. The existence of such a policy would encourage more young researchers to join, they will feel protected.

Also I think what is said here applies to other libraries in the community and not just CSLib.

Hi all,
Some clarifications:

  • In general, I agree we need to write down some rules. I don't think Mathlib's style guide are enough to deal with this. We need to ensure professional integrity.
  • As I mentioned before in private, I have no intentions of merging any of the mentioned PRs on a new algorithm framework until we sort out which solution(s) we want. Unfortunately that discussion raised another issue, which is that sometimes it's hard for me (or other relevant maintainers in general) to get straight answers to key questions for deciding among proposals.
  • Once we figure out which solution(s) we want, before merging anything, we will review what should build on what, which authors should be mentioned, git history, etc.
  • I'm currently the only one who can merge a new algorithm framework, so I'm the one who needs to be convinced of both the code and the ethics behind a coherent proposal. I'm not gonna merge code if I have reason to think any of these two are not in order.
  • We fully realise that authorship of work is connected to careers, and of the fact that especially young researchers need protection.

That said,

  • The discussion about algorithms has revealed that we have another problem: people can start long discussions that make it much more difficult to see precise answers to what questions the maintainers have. This can make discussions go stale. We need to address this, too.
  • I've seen messages by non-maintainers stating that the scope of CSLib is such and such, or that people should contribute to an approach instead of another, or similar. This needs to be addressed, too.
  • Writing down things will be good both for people to know they're protected, and to actually guarantee protection also when I'm not gonna be the only one to make this kind of decisions on new things (which is hopefully soon, and writing things down will be helpful towards that goal as well).

In a nutshell, we're very aware that matters of ethics and 'work environment' are extremely important, and we're working on it. Please be patient. We're not rushing so that we can get it as right as we can. Once we have a proposal, I'll make a draft PR to discuss it.

Another problem we're thinking about is that sometimes, people copy-paste code to create extensions/variants. This will happen a lot in logic, languages, and other models. For example, taking from work I've contributed to, we have HML, so one could extend it to implement mu-calculus. Some people have asked the authors of the code they're copy-pasting and added them as authors to their own files. But maybe a sort of standard citation system/guideline, like we do in papers, is in order to obtain a clean solution here.

Thank you so much Fabrizio. I also wish to request clarity on contributions w.r.t

  1. Distinctions between conceptual, design, and implementation contributions.
  2. Order of file authors when a new PR is made to replace an old one.
  3. Copyright in files.
  4. Norms on opening new PRs which claim to improve on existing PRs. For example, prior discussions, possibility of addressing issues through reviews, Zulip.

Update. Some work still needs to be done (you'll notice some 'notes' and missing parts) but we're making progress here: https://github.com/leanprover/cslib/compare/main...contributing

The CSLib SG will meet again today to discuss additions and we'll start a discussion here once we have covered enough points.

Notice from the Zulip Moderators

The Code of Conduct team has received and carefully verified information regarding conduct in the discussions mentioned in this thread, and related discussions on CSLib. These matters have been dealt with in private, in order to protect everybody involved. However, during this process we have also noticed that some accusations have been made in public, some explicitly (towards @Kim Morrison) and some implicitly (towards @Chris Henson).

The moderators would therefore like to state that we found nothing to criticise about how @Kim Morrison and @Chris Henson have behaved. To the contrary, they have been consistently professional and constructive.

We appreciate everyone’s efforts in keeping this a welcoming community. If you have any concerns, please contact the Code of Conduct team or Zulip moderators.

Response to the aforementioned notice (esp. “professional conduct”)

I will counter the aforementioned statement by saying that

  1. I am the complainant. This is amply clear from the top message in the thread.
  2. I made no complaint about Chris Henson.
  3. The CoC was offered and declined to take a timeline of events from my side. Therefore they haven’t heard my side of the story.
  4. The CoC has described the following conduct as "consistently professional and constructive": someone taking in-progress work whose first PR was nearly complete and producing (with Claude), first a work they claim to be superior to mine, and later in the process of addressing defects in their work, an essentially identical version to mine with :
    a. Their employer as the copyright holder.
    b. Themselves as, at first sole author, and then after requests by maintainers (1.5 months later) as first author.
    c. Showing over the span of two PRs a poor understanding of the contents or the goals of the PR.
    This sounds like an amazing precedent to set, on everything from PR duplication to authorship practices, which is what I hoped this thread would address. I hope new contributors are watching and take appropriate precautions, especially when they are asked to make dependent PRs, all the way upto claiming copyright with AI written code.
  5. Further in their private conversations with me, the CoC has revealed a clear lack of understanding of the contents of the dispute they are judging while making authoritative statements. Further the committee continues to insist that the authorship of files is merely an assumption of responsibility and not claims to originality. One wonders whether this is sufficient excuse to make duplicates of existing PRs with oneself as author, not to mention take copyright (even if the covered content is open source) especially with such big overlap.
  6. Given that all parties in this dispute are known publicly through their posts, it is unclear whom the CoC claims to protect. They are certainly not protecting the affected party here (me) and heaping praises on the accused.

This response will be shared with others outside this forum at my discretion. A meme posted by someone on the lean discord appears to aptly and succinctly describe the aforementioned notice.

Most of this is handled by Apache 2.0. Technically there may be some ambiguity, but it explicitly covers ideas which are discussed in communication channels such as the Zulip. If you don't want to license your ideas permissively, don't grant an Apache 2.0 license to them. That's what you're doing when you submit a PR or talk about something in this channel, as far as I can tell from reading the license.

This is a feature, not a bug: we can spend less time talking about whose ideas are whose, since we've licensed them to each other permissively. Instead, we can talk about which ideas are best.

This is all orthogonal to academic integrity, which is an important discussion for a different forum.

Samuel you are completely misreading this issue. An open source license does not override academic or oss norms in any way. Quite the opposite actually. For the same reason you cannot take a paper and create a very similar version with your own name on it even though it may have a preprint with a Creative Commons license. Licenses are limited to legal liability. Further, and completely orthogonal to the above, apache actually has an attribution condition and requires a clear statement of changes made from the original version. Furthermore code is different from ideas it encodes. Specifically w.r.t copyright:

4 c)
You must retain, in the Source form of any Derivative Works that You distribute, all copyright, patent, trademark, and attribution notices from the Source form of the Work
(deleted)
Lastly, academic and OSS ethics is very specifically the topic of this particular discussion that I started . I’d appreciate not having it distracted by orthogonal licensing issues.

My point is: adjudicating academic ownership should not be the responsibility of the maintainers here. Cslib is an open-source project with a specific license, not a journal or conference.

The maintainers already have a lot on their hands reviewing PRs and doing maintenance work. I think they can set clear norms for attribution and contribution etiquette without being expected to resolve academic ownership disputes. I think the contribution guidelines Fabrizio shared go a long way to doing that.

I have made my point above. This is very clearly an academic project. It models itself on mathlib. A lot of work that goes into optimal formalisation in areas that have never seen much formalisation. It is research even if it happens out in the open. It specifically encodes academic material. There is precedent with content pushed to or upstreamed to mathlib being done so as part of publishable work in ITP and CPP and other venues.

I saw cslib#372, thought it wasn't great, but that no one was willing to argue with Shreyas about it, for presumably inferrable reasons. So I proposed an alternative implementation in cslib#376, that I thought was better (and still do, and still think Shreyas has never responded to my criticism of his version -- that there is no type whose inhabitation corresponds to belief that a fixed external program runs in a specified time). Shreyas immediately started complaining about authorship concerns (in my mind, saying "no, this is bad, here's something better" does not warrant adding academic attribution beyond pointing at it :woman_shrugging:), and hasn't stopped. It's painful and unpleasant to work in CSLib as a result. Subsequently @Eric Wieser, @Fabrizio Montesi , and @Sebastian Graf reviewed the PRs, and recommended that I make cslib#401, which avoids all the QueryTree and Prog monad excesses and just works directly with a free monad --- a basic idea which no one here can claim any credit for, I think :-). cslib#401 includes authorship lines attributing to anyone who was I aware had talked about the topic of each file. In my mind authorship lines in Mathlib and CSLlib are more about attributing maintenance obligations than credit, so I'm very happy to "share"! I haven't had time to go back to polishing cslib#401, and indeed have been avoiding doing so because of the excessive noise here in CSLib.
You challenged me to produce a lower bound. I have produced a lower bound of comparison sorting, albeit GPT derived, because I was in the midst of a workshop

You are claiming as your contribution removing an abbrev from my PR, because Prog is a type synonym for FreeM. The fact that you call "removing Prog" a contribution only adds more evidence to my claim that you don't understand the content involved. You are using the exact same "Prog excesses" you claim to be improving.

Extended rebuttal of the utterly silly claims above.

Since you started cslib#401, you have :
1. Removed QueryTree and used a FreeM directly for lower bounds. So I wonder how your claim about the superiority of cslib#376 or cslib#401 holds when you need to use my model for lower bounds. Even when starting the PR you removed all the extraneous monadic machinery related to mvcgen and used FreeM for upper bounds. Again abbrev Prog := FreeM
2. You have switched from a state monad to a Tally monad to TimeM.
This is exactly what cslib#372 already does. Every change Eric and Sebastian have suggested has brought your PR closer to mine.
3. Your core lower bound proof is an imitation of the one in cslib#372 (well GPT came up with that actually, with some idea prompting on my end) which was posted hours before yours. The input/model hiding idea is a very broad idea that at least goes back to Knuth. It has many modern variants. I did skip writing a stronger bound because my proof satisfied your challenge. My PR actually has two variants of the proof.
4. Further you made your lower bound challenge in the context of cslib#376 after which you implicitly switched to my FreeM model for lower bounds (this was the origin of QueryTree), already in cslib#376. This was your supposedly superior model which is strictly less general than free monads of CSLib#372.
5. You have completely avoided the fact I was the first to point out the redundancy of your query tree in your PR. The reason is because your PR is exactly using my model and in my PR, I simply get the query trace from the Free monad.
6. Your PR CSLib#401 description claims to combine monad polymorphism with free monads. At this point you are not even using your claimed version of monad polymorphism. The idea is entirely free monads. Basically it is entirely cslib#372. Whatever original hybrid idea you had has completely disappeared into mine. And I actually told you this would happen in the other thread. Let me explain why. When you use a Free monad, you are already functor polymorphic.
7. Your PR description in cslib#401 is just how every free monad DSL works: write a syntax tree in the do notation and then evaluate with models/oracles. In literally every free monad program you “produce your query plan” before “the oracle is supplied”. This is literally happening already in CSLib#372. You could shorten the entire second paragraph with “this is a free monad DSL” and replace the first paragraph with “this is the free monad dsl of CSLib#372, but splits the eval and time function out of the Model structure”. That would be accurate and completely describe CSLib#401.

Currently if you take my PR and write the explicit structures of upper and lower bound (which is a bit of polishing if at all, and unsuitable in full generality), you get your PR. The fact you do not realise this adds weight to my case. One exception is, I do the sensible thing of coupling costs with evaluations because that is the definition of an algorithmic model, of which I hope to build a top down web.

I am sorry that the response has to be this long. Sadly, egregiously wrong claims require a long response. It is extremely distressing to contribute when someone repeatedly makes silly claims that they have a better model when it is for all practical purposes a carbon copy of mine at this point, and they show such a clear lack of understanding of my work and worse still, their own.

Regarding 1. and 2., I think the claim is that using FreeM + TimeM together to measure query complexity is the "basic idea which no one here can claim any credit for" (though I believe I requested this strategy on both 372 and 401, and so neither of you copied this from the other).

At this point cslib#401 is a cosmetic change (largely negative ones) over cslib#372 and you have confirmed by your claim of "removing Prog" as an achievement, that you do not understand my PR or your own for that matter. Your PR has a slightly cleaner "final" version of the sorting bound, but is nearly identical in its essence. The meaningful thing to do is to merge mine, and borrow the positive cosmetic changes from yours on top of cslib#372.

@Eric Wieser : The change to TimeM that you suggested already landed before Feb 26/27 in my PR. I was on the overnight from Munich to Bologna iirc. We were already discussing stable sort, which incidentally has landed in Algolean recently.
